data.author: researcher-mathematical
data.title: Learned initializer + log-space Gauss-Newton/LM refinement reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
data.hypothesis: The map theta -> F(theta) is smooth and locally well-conditioned (median Fisher condition 48), with noise sigma=1e-3. So a few LM steps started from a cheap data-driven estimate converge to the per-sample MLE. The MLE's error should approach the CRB rel_l2 floor of about 0.019. Hybrid kernel_ridge init with 10 LM iterations in log(k) will give val rel_l2 < 0.035, at least 5x better than any pure library regressor of similar cost.
data.motivation: The forward operator is a 4-parameter, cheap, fully known explicit FD solver. The diagnostics show every parameter is locally identifiable, with CRB relative std between 0.005 and 0.022. A purely learned regressor trained on 3000 samples in a 4-D box has approximation error that likely sits well above the CRB. Local Gauss-Newton removes that approximation error, provided it starts inside the basin of attraction. A learned initializer supplies that start and avoids the cost of multistart. A log transform matches the multiplicative scale of conductivity, enforces positivity, and makes the Jacobian columns more uniform across [0.5, 2]. k1 and k4 are the least determined because their segments are far from the Gaussian pulse at x=0.5, so heat reaches them late and weakly.
assumptions: The harness forward model is the same simulator that generated the data: same grid, dt, initial condition and sensor indices.
The explicit scheme is stable for k up to 2: dt*k_max/dx^2 <= 1/2.
Misfit has a single dominant basin around the truth over most of the box; kernel ridge init lands inside it.
Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian, so unweighted least squares is the MLE.

evidence.claim: Local identifiability is good: median Fisher condition number 48 and CRB rel_l2 floor about 0.0186, well below the 0.05 target.
Under a tangential cone condition and an initial guess close enough to the solution, LM with discrepancy stopping terminates and is regularizing.
With noisy data and stopping before k*, LM iterates stay in a neighbourhood of x0 and terminate in finitely many steps.
k1 and k4 have CRB rel std about 0.02, so per-parameter error near the boundary segments limits the achievable rel_l2; the floor is not zero.

citations.note: Hanke's tangential cone condition is local and unverified for this discrete heat map. Smoothness of F in k and the low condition number make it plausible near the truth. The closeness requirement on u0 is what the learned initializer is meant to satisfy. Our problem is finite-dimensional, which is easier than the infinite-dimensional setting.

Its assumptions (ALM, A5) are local Lipschitz and cone-type conditions, not verified here. It only guarantees boundedness and termination, not CRB-level accuracy. The harness uses bound-constrained LM with a fixed iteration count rather than the discrepancy principle.

data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid against its own kernel_ridge init. Check whether the per-parameter relative errors of k1..k4 track the CRB ordering (k1, k4 > k2, k3) with magnitudes within 2x of the CRB. The hypothesis is refuted if val rel_l2 >= 0.035, or if refinement improves on the init by less than 2x. Either outcome would indicate bad basins, inconsistency between the forward model and the data, or failure of LM convergence.

feasibility.notes: Per sample: about 10 iterations, each needing a Jacobian (about 5 forward solves of a 40x200 explicit scheme), so about 50-100 cheap solves. For roughly 1500 samples this is vectorizable and should fit within 120s. Kernel ridge on 3000 samples is negligible.

data.if_fails: If rel_l2 stays near the init, the learned initializer is outside the LM basin or the forward model is mismatched with the data. In that case increase extra_starts or check the residual norm against the expected sqrt(m)*sigma. If error is dominated by k1 and k4 at the CRB level, the floor is fundamental and only a prior-informed estimator (proposal 2) can help.

data.author: researcher-mathematical
data.title: Bayesian MMSE (posterior mean under the box prior) beats the MLE on rel_l2 because CRB-limited segments k1 and k4 benefit from prior shrinkage
data.hypothesis: rel_l2 is a squared-error-type loss. The prior is known exactly (i.i.d. uniform on [0.5, 2]). So the posterior mean is the Bayes-optimal estimator and is not bound by the unbiased CRB. Pure physics LM in log space with multistart 3, followed by importance-sampled posterior mean on the Laplace approximation, will reach val rel_l2 < 0.03. It will also be at least 5% better than the same pipeline with estimator=mode, with the gain concentrated in k1 and k4 and in samples near the box bounds.
data.motivation: The CRB applies only to unbiased estimators. With a bounded uniform prior, the MLE projected onto the box is biased near the bounds and has high variance in the weakly observed edge segments. The MMSE estimator under the true prior minimizes expected squared error, so in expectation it cannot be worse than the MLE. The Laplace approximation is accurate because the posterior is nearly Gaussian at sigma=1e-3 and cond about 48, and importance sampling corrects for box truncation. Multistart replaces the learned init and tests whether the misfit landscape is unimodal enough for physics alone. This proposal needs no training data at all, which also separates physics error from learning error.
assumptions: The prior stated in the problem is the true data-generating prior for val and test.
The posterior is close to Gaussian in log(k) near the mode, so a Laplace proposal gives low-variance importance weights.
Multistart with 3 starts finds the global mode for most samples.
The forward model matches the data generator.

evidence.claim: The Bayes posterior mean minimizes expected squared error under the true prior, so it can fall below the unbiased CRB floor of about 0.0186.
At sigma=1e-3 the posterior is sharply concentrated (relative std 0.005-0.022), so prior shrinkage gains may be small except near the bounds and for k1 and k4.
LM converges from nearby starts under local cone conditions, which supports finding the mode reliably for the Laplace step.

citations.note: This supports only the mode-finding stage, and only locally. It says nothing about the global basin from multistart, nor about optimality of the posterior mean. Its assumptions are not verified for this map.
A regularization property of LM with singular scaling. It is relevant only if the Jacobian is near-singular. Here cond is about 48, so its main use-case (null-space handling) probably does not apply.

data.falsifiable_test: Run the same configuration with estimator=mode as a paired control on the same val samples. Report rel_l2 overall, per parameter, and stratified by whether the true k lies within 0.1 of a bound. The hypothesis is refuted if posterior_mean is not at least 5% better than mode, or if overall val rel_l2 >= 0.03. If multistart samples disagree on the mode for more than 5% of samples, the unimodality assumption is falsified.

feasibility.notes: 3 starts x 25 iterations x Jacobian per sample, plus 128 forward solves for importance sampling, across val and test samples. This may approach the 120s per-experiment limit. If it is too slow, reduce to multistart 2 with iters 15; LM typically converges in fewer than 10 iterations when cond is about 48.

data.if_fails: If mode and posterior_mean tie, the posterior is so concentrated that the CRB/MLE is effectively Bayes-optimal and the hybrid approach (proposal 1) is the cheaper equivalent. If both exceed 0.03 while residuals are at the noise level, the floor is intrinsic. If residuals exceed sqrt(m)*sigma, the forward model is mismatched or the basins are bad.

data.title: Posterior-mean (MMSE) under the box prior beats the MLE on the poorly determined end segments
data.hypothesis: Because rel_l2 is a squared-error metric and the prior is a bounded uniform box, the importance-sampled posterior mean should beat the LS mode, especially on k1 and k4. Prediction: at least 8% lower val rel_l2 than the best data-driven method and below 0.025 overall. The gain should concentrate in samples whose true k1 or k4 lies within about 2 CRB standard deviations of 0.5 or 2.0.
data.motivation: This is a competing explanation for any gap above the CRB. In proposal 1 the gap is attributed to initializer or basin failures. Here it is attributed to the estimator itself: the bounded MLE clips at the box edges, while the Bayes posterior mean is the L2-optimal estimator under the true prior. The data were generated from that prior, which makes this a controlled test. Pure physics with multistart from the prior centre also serves as a control for whether a learned initializer is even necessary.
assumptions: Train, val and test parameters are drawn i.i.d. uniform on [0.5, 2]^4, matching the stated prior.
The Laplace proposal in log space covers the posterior well enough that importance weights do not collapse; the effective sample size stays above about 10 for at least 95% of samples.
Multistart LM from 3 starts finds the global mode for nearly all samples without a learned initializer, since the condition number is moderate.
The forward model matches the data generator, as in proposal 1.

evidence.claim: Under squared-error loss with the correct prior, the posterior mean is the Bayes-optimal estimator, so it can only improve average MSE over the mode. This is a decision-theory fact; no retrieved ref covers it.
The CRB relative std for k1 and k4 is about 2%. With a box width of 1.5, only a small fraction of samples lie near a bound, so the expected gain may be small, perhaps under 5%.
The posterior is nearly Gaussian in the small-noise regime with moderate conditioning, which supports Laplace-based importance sampling.

data.author: researcher-exploratory
data.title: Amortised-then-exact: an MLP on log features as a global initialiser, LM posterior-mean refinement as the corrector
data.hypothesis: A purely data-driven regressor (torch MLP on log-temperature features, with log targets) will stall well above the CRB floor, at val rel_l2 around 0.04-0.08, because 3000 samples are too few to learn the inverse map to noise-limited precision in 4D. Using that same network only as an initialiser for 10 LM iterations with the posterior-mean correction will cut its val rel_l2 by at least 40%, landing below 0.03. It will do this with fewer forward evaluations than cold-start physics, because the learned initialiser removes the need for multistarts.
data.motivation: This combines two traditions: amortised simulation-based inference and classical variational data assimilation. Each has a characteristic failure. The network is robust globally, but its precision is limited by approximation and estimation error. LM is precise locally, but it can be trapped in a poor basin when started far away. The proposal tests whether these failures are complementary. Log features make sense physically: the solution decays roughly exponentially in time at rates that scale with k, so log u is closer to linear in log k. The task could be framed as 'choose the best regressor', but the network actually only needs to land within the LM basin of attraction. If that is true, a cheap network is enough and the remaining error is set by the likelihood rather than the learner.
assumptions: The MLP's errors are small enough (relative error up to about 10%) that LM converges to the global basin from the MLP's estimate.

The log feature transform is defined: sensor readings stay positive or are shifted/clipped by the harness. Near-zero late-time readings with noise of 1e-3 could make log features noisy or undefined. If the harness clips them, information may be distorted.
Training data come from the same simulator as the val data and from the same prior, so the amortised initialiser has no distribution shift.
LM refinement cost with 10 iterations and no extra starts fits within the 120 s per-experiment limit alongside MLP training.

evidence.claim: The mean-predictor baseline is 0.33 and the CRB floor is 0.019. That large gap means the inverse map is informative, and a learned model can capture most of it without reaching the floor.
A moderate Fisher conditioning (about 48) implies the local quadratic basin is reasonably wide, so a learned estimate with a few percent error should lie inside it.

If the cold-start physics method (proposal 1) already reaches the floor with 3 multistarts, the learned initialiser adds no accuracy and only saves compute. In that case the accuracy part of this hypothesis would be redundant.
Late-time readings near zero give log features with a heavy-tailed noise distribution. That could hurt the MLP more than raw features would.

citations.note: This is a time-Lipschitz bound for viscosity solutions of nonlocal integro-differential parabolic equations. Its setting (censored subdiffusion, superfractional gradient terms) does not match the local divergence-form heat equation with discontinuous k used here. The harness also flags that it uses full spatial data. It is cited only to state explicitly that it does not justify smoothness of the sensor time series here, and no claim depends on it.

data.falsifiable_test: Report val rel_l2 for two things: the MLP initialiser alone, and the hybrid after refinement. The hypothesis is falsified if any of these hold: (a) the hybrid's val rel_l2 >= 0.03; (b) the hybrid improves on the MLP-only val rel_l2 by less than 40%; or (c) the MLP-only val rel_l2 is already <= 0.025, meaning the 'learner stalls' premise is wrong. Separately, compare forward-call counts with proposal 1: the hybrid should use fewer.

feasibility.notes: Training an MLP on 3000 samples on CPU should take about 20-40 s. Refinement is about 10 LM iterations plus 128 importance samples per val sample, with a single start. If the 120 s per-experiment limit is at risk, drop epochs to 100 or posterior_samples to 64.

data.if_fails: (a) If the hybrid does not beat 0.03 but proposal 1 does, the learned initialiser is placing LM in wrong basins, which points to a systematic MLP bias near the box bounds. The fix would be extra_starts = 1. (b) If the MLP alone is already near the floor, the inverse map is simple enough to amortise. Then a cheaper pure-learning method is the efficient choice, and the claim of complementary failures is refuted for this problem. (c) If log features underperform raw features at the initialiser stage, the low-signal late-time readings are harmful and should be removed or treated with a sqrt transform.
